newsitem.title: LEBANON: Arab banks can boost foreign capital inflow - report. [CORRECTED 19:53 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Arab banks can boost foreign capital inflow - report. [CORRECTED 19:53 GMT]

text.p: The Arab banking sector has a vital role to play in increasing the flow of foreign investment into the Arab World, the Union of Arab Banks said on Wednesday.

"One of the current and future challenges facing Arab banks is their ability to capitalise on growing international interest in the Arab region as a worthy investment area," it said in a report to an Arab banking conference in Beirut.

"The Arab banks are urged, in view of this fact, to work to increase the volume of investment flows into the Arab world on several sectors, the first of which is developing the base of their investment products and instruments," the report added.
It said direct foreign investments into Arab states rose to $1.8 billion in 1994 from $1.7 billion in 1993, but both figures were less than one percent of private international investments.
The Arab banking sector should become the main player and the motor of the Arab capital markets and should issue eurobonds on international capital markets, the report said.
"These steps by the banks can boost the Arab World's position as an important investment region and contribute to attracting both expatriate and foreign capital and investments," it said.
Arab banks' share in financing Arab economies increased by 14.9 percent in 1995 to $254 billion, mainly through project finance and syndicated loans for major investment projects, the report added.
Total deposits (corrects from assets) of Arab banks rose by 20.7 percent in 1995 to $289 billion compared with a 6.1 percent increase in 1994.

This was partly due to the return of expatriate money, increased inter-Arab investments, high interest rates coupled with monetary stability in many Arab countries, and the introduction of several new financial investment instruments.
"There are also good results from economic reform programmes...in a number of Arab countries," it added.

The report said Arab banks' total external investments rose by 3.8 percent in 1995 to $80.4 billion following a retreat of 3.6 percent in 1994. The investments were part of some $650 billion of Arab capital invested outside the region.
The report said that in 1995 the assets of Arab banks rose 14.2 percent to $496 billion compared with 5.8 percent in 1994 and 5.1 percent a year earlier.

"This reflects increased activity by Arab banks in general in the fields of economic investments, financing of projects and external trade, financial intermediation and dealing in some banking and financial instruments introduced recently internationally," the report added.

Lebanese banks topped the list for growth in the banking sector with 23.5 percent, followed by banks in Morocco, Egypt, Tunisia and Jordan at 13.5 percent, 11.9 percent, 11.8 percent and 10.7 percent respectively.
